questions.q: What components make up a nucleoside?
options: A nitrogenous base and a pentose sugar
A nitrogenous base and a phosphate group
A pentose sugar and a phosphate group
A purine ring and a fatty acid
questions.explain: A nucleoside consists of a nitrogenous base (purine or pyrimidine) covalently attached to a pentose sugar (ribose or 2-deoxyribose) via a beta-N-glycosidic bond. Adding one or more phosphate groups converts it into a nucleotide.

open.q: Which two chemical components form a nucleoside?
accept: purine or pyrimidine base and ribose or deoxyribose

questions.q: Which nucleoside is formed when adenine is linked to D-ribose?
questions.explain: Adenine attached to ribose is adenosine (and to deoxyribose is deoxyadenosine). Guanosine contains guanine, cytidine contains cytosine, and uridine contains uracil.

open.q: What is the name of the ribonucleoside composed of adenine and ribose?

questions.q: Which pyrimidine base is 5-methyluracil?
questions.explain: Thymine is chemically 5-methyl-2,4-dioxopyrimidine, differing from uracil by a methyl group at position 5. It is found predominantly in DNA rather than RNA.

open.q: Which pyrimidine base has the chemical name 5-methyluracil?

questions.q: At which carbon of the pentose sugar is a nitrogenous base attached in a standard nucleotide?
questions.explain: The nitrogenous base forms a beta-N-glycosidic bond with C-1 (the anomeric carbon) of ribose or 2-deoxyribose. Phosphate groups esterify at the 5-hydroxyl (or 3-hydroxyl) position.

open.q: To which sugar carbon atom is the nitrogenous base joined in a nucleoside or nucleotide?

questions.q: Which bond connects the alpha and beta phosphate groups in a nucleoside triphosphate such as ATP?
questions.explain: The bond between the first (alpha) and sugar hydroxyl is a phosphoester bond, whereas the bonds linking adjacent phosphates (alpha-beta and beta-gamma) are high-energy phosphoanhydride bonds. Hydrolysis of phosphoanhydride bonds releases substantial free energy.

open.q: What type of high-energy bond joins adjacent phosphate groups in ATP?

questions.q: Which cyclic nucleotide acts as a major intracellular second messenger activated by adenylyl cyclase?
questions.explain: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into cyclic AMP (3,5-cyclic adenosine monophosphate), which activates protein kinase A (PKA) to mediate hormonal signals. Cyclic GMP (cGMP) is another second messenger synthesized by guanylyl cyclase.

open.q: Which cyclic nucleotide second messenger is synthesized from ATP by adenylyl cyclase?

questions.q: Which activated nucleotide sugar serves as the glucosyl donor in glycogen synthesis?
questions.explain: UDP-glucose (uridine diphosphate glucose) is the activated glucose donor used by glycogen synthase to add glucose residues to growing glycogen chains. CDP-diacylglycerol and CDP-choline participate in phospholipid synthesis.

open.q: Which nucleotide-linked sugar donates glucose units during glycogen synthesis?

questions.q: Which nucleotide derivative serves as a major biological methyl group donor in transmethylation reactions?
questions.explain: S-adenosylmethionine is formed from ATP and methionine and contains a sulfonium ion with an activated methyl group easily transferred by methyltransferases. Demethylation yields S-adenosylhomocysteine.

open.q: Which nucleotide-containing coenzyme donates methyl groups in metabolic transmethylation reactions?

questions.q: According to Chargaff's rules for double-stranded DNA, what is the molar relationship between purines and pyrimidines?
options: Purines are twice as abundant as pyrimidines
questions.explain: In double-stranded DNA, adenine pairs with thymine ([A] = [T]) and guanine pairs with cytosine ([G] = [C]), so total purines equal total pyrimidines. Base composition varies between species.

open.q: What relationship holds between total purine and total pyrimidine content in double-stranded DNA under Chargaff's rules?

questions.q: What is the orientation of the two complementary strands in the Watson-Crick DNA double helix?
options: Parallel (both run 5-to-3 in the same direction)
Circular with no free 5 or 3 ends
questions.explain: The two strands of double-stranded DNA run in opposite (antiparallel) directions: one strand has a 5-to-3 phosphodiester polarity while its complement runs 3-to-5. This allows base pairing across the helix axis.

open.q: How are the two strands of a DNA double helix oriented relative to each other in terms of 5-to-3 directionality?

questions.q: Which conformation is the predominant right-handed double helix of DNA under physiological conditions?
questions.explain: B-DNA is the standard right-handed double helix under physiological salt and hydration conditions, with about 10 to 10.5 base pairs per turn. Z-DNA is a left-handed zig-zag helix favored by alternating purine-pyrimidine sequences.

open.q: Which form of double-helical DNA is the standard right-handed structure under physiological conditions?

questions.q: Which DNA conformation forms a left-handed double helix with a zig-zag sugar-phosphate backbone?
questions.explain: Z-DNA is a left-handed double helix with a zig-zag backbone and alternating guanine (syn) and cytosine (anti) conformations. A-DNA is a wider, right-handed form seen in dehydrated DNA or RNA-DNA hybrids.

open.q: Which left-handed double-helical form of DNA has a zig-zag backbone?

questions.q: Between two double-stranded DNA molecules of equal length, which one will have a higher melting temperature (Tm)?
options: The molecule with a higher guanine-cytosine (G-C) percentage
The molecule with a higher adenine-thymine (A-T) percentage
The molecule with fewer phosphodiester bonds
The molecule lacking hydrogen bonds between bases
questions.explain: Each G-C base pair has three hydrogen bonds compared with two in an A-T base pair, and base-stacking interactions also differ. Higher G-C content increases thermal stability and raises the melting temperature (Tm).

open.q: Which base composition feature increases the melting temperature (Tm) of double-stranded DNA?
accept: more guanine and cytosine base pairs

questions.q: At what ultraviolet wavelength do purine and pyrimidine bases in nucleic acids maximally absorb light?
questions.explain: Aromatic purine and pyrimidine rings absorb ultraviolet light maximally at 260 nm, whereas aromatic amino acids (tryptophan and tyrosine) in proteins absorb maximally around 280 nm. The A260/A280 ratio assesses nucleic acid purity.

open.q: At what approximate ultraviolet wavelength do nucleic acids show peak absorbance?

questions.q: What happens to ultraviolet absorbance at 260 nm when double-stranded DNA denatures into single strands (hyperchromic effect)?
options: Absorbance increases because base stacking decreases
Absorbance decreases because bases become covalently linked
Absorbance shifts exclusively to visible red light
questions.explain: In native double-stranded DNA, stacked bases partially quench UV absorption; separation of strands during denaturation (melting) unstacks the bases and increases A260, known as the hyperchromic effect.

open.q: Why does UV absorbance at 260 nm rise when double-stranded DNA melts into single strands?

questions.q: Which group of basic proteins packages eukaryotic DNA into nucleosomes?
questions.explain: Histones are small, positively charged (basic) proteins rich in lysine and arginine that bind the negatively charged sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA. Eight histone subunits form the nucleosome core particle.

open.q: Which positively charged nuclear proteins form the core around which eukaryotic DNA wraps in nucleosomes?

questions.q: Which histone protein seals DNA where it enters and exits the nucleosome core and facilitates higher-order chromatin compaction?
questions.explain: Linker histone H1 binds DNA at the entry and exit points of the nucleosome octamer (composed of two each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4). It helps condense nucleosome arrays into higher-order chromatin structures.

open.q: Which linker histone binds at the entry and exit sites of DNA on the nucleosome?

questions.q: How does acetylation of lysine residues on histone tails generally affect chromatin structure and gene transcription?
options: Neutralizes positive charge to loosen chromatin and promote transcription
Increases positive charge to tighten chromatin and silence transcription
Cleaves the DNA backbone into short fragments
questions.explain: Histone acetyltransferases add acetyl groups to lysine epsilon-amino groups, removing positive charge that attracts negatively charged DNA. This relaxes chromatin into a more open euchromatin state accessible to transcription.

open.q: How does histone lysine acetylation typically influence chromatin compactness?

questions.q: Which form of chromatin is generally less condensed, transcriptionally active, and replicates earlier in S phase?
questions.explain: Euchromatin is dispersed and open in interphase nuclei and contains most actively transcribed genes. Heterochromatin is densely packed and generally transcriptionally inactive.

open.q: Which term describes dispersed, transcriptionally active eukaryotic chromatin?

questions.q: Which type of RNA carries genetic codons from nuclear DNA to cytoplasmic ribosomes for protein synthesis?
questions.explain: Messenger RNA (mRNA) is transcribed from DNA templates and specifies the amino acid sequence of polypeptides via three-nucleotide codons. tRNA brings amino acids, and rRNA forms structural and catalytic parts of ribosomes.

open.q: Which class of RNA carries codon information from DNA to the ribosome to direct polypeptide synthesis?

questions.q: Which structural feature of transfer RNA (tRNA) base-pairs with a complementary codon on mRNA during translation?
questions.explain: Each tRNA molecule contains an anticodon triplet that pairs antiparallel with the mRNA codon, while its 3-CCA terminus carries the corresponding amino acid. tRNA also contains modified nucleosides such as pseudouridine and dihydrouridine.

open.q: Which sequence region on a tRNA molecule recognizes and pairs with an mRNA codon?

questions.q: Which RNA species catalyzes peptide bond formation (peptidyl transferase activity) on the ribosome?
questions.explain: Large-subunit ribosomal RNA acts as a ribozyme catalyzing peptide bond formation between the aminoacyl-tRNA and peptidyl-tRNA. Proteins stabilize ribosome architecture but rRNA provides the peptidyl transferase catalysis.

open.q: Which type of RNA serves as the catalytic ribozyme for peptide bond formation in ribosomes?

questions.q: Which small RNA complexes with proteins to form spliceosomes that remove introns from eukaryotic pre-mRNA?
questions.explain: Small nuclear RNAs (such as U1, U2, U4, U5, and U6 snRNAs) combine with proteins into snRNPs that assemble into the spliceosome to excise introns and join exons. This occurs in the nucleus prior to mRNA export.

open.q: Which class of nuclear RNA participates in pre-mRNA splicing within the spliceosome?

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting committed step of de novo purine nucleotide synthesis?
questions.explain: Glutamine-phosphoribosylpyrophosphate (PRPP) amidotransferase transfers an amino group from glutamine to PRPP to form 5-phosphoribosylamine, the committed step of de novo purine synthesis. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II initiates de novo pyrimidine synthesis.

open.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed step of de novo purine biosynthesis using PRPP and glutamine?

questions.q: A male child presents with developmental delay, spasticity, self-injurious behavior, choreoathetosis, and hyperuricemia with gouty tophi. Deficiency of which purine salvage enzyme causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?
questions.explain: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked disorder caused by deficiency or absence of HGPRT, preventing salvage of hypoxanthine to IMP and guanine to GMP. Elevated PRPP drives de novo purine synthesis and excess purines are degraded to uric acid.

open.q: Deficiency of which purine salvage enzyme causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with hyperuricemia and neurological features?

questions.q: An infant presents with severe recurrent viral, bacterial, and fungal infections from early infancy, failure to thrive, and marked lymphopenia affecting both T and B lymphocytes. Deficiency of which enzyme in purine catabolism causes this form of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)?
questions.explain: Adenosine deaminase deficiency leads to accumulation of adenosine and deoxyadenosine, which is phosphorylated to dATP. Elevated dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and impairs DNA synthesis/lymphocyte proliferation, causing severe combined immunodeficiency.

open.q: Deficiency of which purine-metabolizing enzyme causes an autosomal recessive form of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)?

questions.q: What is the final metabolic end product of purine catabolism in humans?
questions.explain: In humans, purines (adenine and guanine) are degraded via xanthine to uric acid, which is excreted in urine. Unlike most other mammals, humans lack uricase (urate oxidase) to convert uric acid into more soluble allantoin.

open.q: Which compound is the terminal end product of purine breakdown in humans?

questions.q: How does allopurinol lower serum uric acid levels in patients with chronic gout?
options: Stimulates renal tubular reabsorption of urate
Converts uric acid into allantoin in the liver
Directly degrades DNA in circulating leukocytes
questions.explain: Allopurinol (and its active metabolite oxypurinol) acts as a suicide/competitive inhibitor of xanthine oxidase, reducing conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid. More soluble hypoxanthine and xanthine are excreted instead.

open.q: Which enzyme does allopurinol inhibit to decrease uric acid production?

questions.q: Which enzyme converts deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP) into deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP) using N5,N10-methylenetetrahydrofolate?
questions.explain: Thymidylate synthase methylates dUMP at position 5 to produce dTMP, utilizing N5,N10-methylenetetrahydrofolate as the one-carbon donor and oxidizing folate to dihydrofolate. It is a major target of anticancer drugs such as 5-fluorouracil.

open.q: Which enzyme methylates dUMP to form dTMP during thymidylate synthesis?

questions.q: Which enzyme converts ribonucleoside diphosphates (NDPs) into deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs) for DNA synthesis?
questions.explain: Ribonucleotide reductase reduces the 2-hydroxyl group on the ribose ring of NDPs (ADP, GDP, CDP, UDP) to form 2-deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs) required for DNA replication. It uses thioredoxin or glutaredoxin as reducing equivalents.

open.q: Which enzyme reduces ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides for DNA synthesis?

questions.q: A patient with gout is treated with a drug that inhibits xanthine oxidase. Which pair of purine metabolites is expected to accumulate upstream of uric acid?
questions.explain: Xanthine oxidase catalyses hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid. Its inhibition reduces urate formation and increases the upstream substrates hypoxanthine and xanthine.

open.q: A patient with gout is treated with a drug that inhibits xanthine oxidase. Which pair of purine metabolites is expected to accumulate upstream of uric acid?

questions.q: A child with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome has hyperuricaemia and self-injurious behaviour. Which enzyme activity is deficient?
questions.explain: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is caused by severe deficiency of HGPRT, a purine salvage enzyme that converts hypoxanthine and guanine to IMP and GMP using PRPP. Increased de novo purine synthesis and degradation contribute to hyperuricaemia.

open.q: A child with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome has hyperuricaemia and self-injurious behaviour. Which enzyme activity is deficient?

questions.q: A patient receiving methotrexate develops impaired DNA synthesis. Which enzyme is directly inhibited by methotrexate?
questions.explain: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, limiting regeneration of tetrahydrofolate derivatives required for one-carbon transfer reactions, including thymidylate and purine synthesis.

open.q: A patient receiving methotrexate develops impaired DNA synthesis. Which enzyme is directly inhibited by methotrexate?

questions.q: A deficiency of orotic acid phosphoribosyltransferase and OMP decarboxylase causes which biochemical pattern?
options: Orotic aciduria with megaloblastic anaemia and no hyperammonaemia
questions.explain: Hereditary orotic aciduria results from deficient UMP synthase activity (orotic acid phosphoribosyltransferase and OMP decarboxylase). Pyrimidine synthesis is impaired, causing orotate accumulation and megaloblastic anaemia; unlike OTC deficiency, hyperammonaemia is absent.

open.q: A deficiency of orotic acid phosphoribosyltransferase and OMP decarboxylase causes which biochemical pattern?
accept: Orotic aciduria with megaloblastic anaemia and no hyperammonaemia

questions.q: Which bond links adjacent nucleotides within a single DNA strand?
questions.explain: Adjacent nucleotides in a DNA strand are joined by 3′–5′ phosphodiester bonds between the 3′ hydroxyl of one sugar and the 5′ phosphate of the next. Hydrogen bonds pair complementary bases across the two strands.

open.q: Which bond links adjacent nucleotides within a single DNA strand?

questions.q: During translation, which RNA molecule carries an amino acid and pairs its anticodon with an mRNA codon?
questions.explain: Transfer RNA acts as an adaptor in translation. Its anticodon base-pairs with the complementary mRNA codon, while its 3′ CCA terminus carries the corresponding amino acid.

open.q: During translation, which RNA molecule carries an amino acid and pairs its anticodon with an mRNA codon?

questions.q: A laboratory assay detects DNA synthesis proceeding discontinuously on one template strand. What are the short newly synthesised fragments called?
questions.explain: DNA polymerase synthesises DNA only in the 5′ to 3′ direction. The lagging strand is therefore made discontinuously as Okazaki fragments, which are subsequently joined by DNA ligase.

open.q: A laboratory assay detects DNA synthesis proceeding discontinuously on one template strand. What are the short newly synthesised fragments called?

questions.q: A patient with severe combined immunodeficiency has a deficiency of adenosine deaminase. Which metabolite accumulation is particularly toxic to lymphocytes?
questions.explain: Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes accumulation of adenosine and deoxyadenosine metabolites. Increased dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, disrupting deoxynucleotide production and impairing lymphocyte DNA synthesis.

open.q: A patient with severe combined immunodeficiency has a deficiency of adenosine deaminase. Which metabolite accumulation is particularly toxic to lymphocytes?
